q: A ball is released from rest in a vacuum. What is its speed after $2.0\,\text{s}$, and what does the number $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ tell?
a: The speed is $v = g\,t = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2 \cdot 2.0\,\text{s} = 19.6\,\text{m/s}$. The number $g$ tells how much the speed increases every second: $9.81\,\text{m/s}$ per second. It is not the speed of the ball.

q: The $(t, v)$ graph of a freely falling object is a straight line. What does its slope tell, and does the line pass through the origin?
a: The slope $\dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$ is the acceleration of free fall $g = 9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$. The line passes through the origin, because the object starts from rest: at the moment $t = 0$ the speed is $v = 0$.

q: In a vacuum a feather and a hammer fall equally fast, but in air the feather falls more slowly. Why?
a: In a vacuum the acceleration of free fall is the same for all objects. In air the air slows a light, wide object, the feather, clearly more than a small, dense object, the hammer. So in air the feather falls more slowly, but in a vacuum the feather and the hammer would fall equally fast.
